records.passage: Its orbit takes it at 7.67 km/s (27,600 km/h; 17,200 mph) roughly every 93 minutes around Earth, 15.5 times a day.

records.claim: The station orbits between 51.64° north and south, at about 400 kilometres (250 miles) above Earth, below the Van Allen radiation belts.
records.passage: The station orbits between 51.64° north and south, at about 400 kilometres (250 miles) above Earth, below the Van Allen radiation belts and most space debris.

narration.text: Why the space station circles Earth every 93 minutes.
That's 15.5 orbits, and sunrises, every day.
It flies at 27,600 kilometres per hour.
Crews aren't beyond gravity; they're constantly falling around Earth.
Days and nights blur, so schedules replace the Sun.
The station is due to operate until the end of 2030.
So living in orbit means living in permanent free fall.
